question.text: A Cat II debt AIF holds a non-performing collateralised debt exposure where the borrower has defaulted. Per IPEV 2022, the valuation approach should reflect:

answer.text: Face value of the debt regardless of default
Pure mark-to-model at the original coupon
Value of underlying collateral, risk of converting collateral to cash, and time required to do so

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Per PDF Section 11.8.3 point 6: 'Non-performing collateralised Debt Investments are often valued based on the VALUE OF UNDERLYING COLLATERAL, the RISK OF CONVERTING the collateral into cash, and the TIME REQUIRED to convert the collateral into cash.' This is essentially a liquidation-based recovery estimate, discounted for execution risk and time. **The Trap:** Face value ignores default; blanket 90% is arbitrary; original coupon mark-to-model ignores the default event. IPEV explicitly points to collateral value + conversion risk + time as the three drivers. **Cross-Exam Context:** XIX-C covers same. Series-XXIV (AML) and Compliance series cover the security-perfection aspect. RBI's IRAC norms (for regulated entities) and Expected Credit Loss under Ind-AS 109 apply parallel logic. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** In Cat II debt deals, insist on perfected security interest (charge filed with ROC, pledge with depository, property mortgage with sub-registrar) BEFORE disbursement. In default scenarios, the valuer will haircut your claim heavily if security perfection is weak.
